clue.text: Drone shot added later — without it, we're lost

definitions.note: a member of the Drones Club, the idle young men's club in P. G. Wodehouse's stories

indicators.note: here 'without' has its old sense of 'outside', so one piece stands around the other

parts.note: a booster is a follow-up vaccine shot given some time after the first dose

indicators.note: lost letters have gone astray, so the words it and we're are jumbled

explanation.surface: A film-maker adds aerial footage in the edit, insisting the picture would be adrift without it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drone' looks like the flying camera of the surface, but it means a Wodehouse idler. 'without' is the old sense of outside, and 'lost' jumbles the two short words into ERTIEW; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's hero is the best-known member of the Drones Club, so a 'Drone' is a fair description of him.

clue.text: Bottler replaced old runner of lines with genuine playwright

indicators.note: replaced means put back differently, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the former operator of Britain's railway lines
echt is German for genuine, a word used in English too

explanation.surface: A bottling plant swaps an old railway firm for something authentic, oddly yielding a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaced' turns BOTTLER into BERTOLT; 'echt' is a German loanword fitting for a German dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: The German author of Mother Courage and The Threepenny Opera was a dramatist.

clue.text: Book encompassing McEwan, Ionesco and Tzara?

indicators.note: encompassing means surrounding, so the novelist's first name sits inside the book

parts.note: Romans is a book of the New Testament
the novelist's first name is Ian

explanation.surface: Asks whether one volume could hold McEwan, Ionesco and Tzara together.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: Eugène Ionesco and Tristan Tzara were both born in Romania.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionesco and Tzara were both born in Romania, so they are examples of its nationals.

clue.text: Forger is turning

annotationWithheld.why: 'Forger is turning (6)' as held: ISRAEL (the forger Lee Israel) fits the crossings, but 'is turning' gives only IS and an indicator, with nothing for the remaining letters; the OCR text seems cut short and there is no scan to check

clue.text: Worthless naval captain departed?

indicators.note: read as 'worth-less', the clue word asks for those five letters to be removed from the captain's name

parts.note: Captain Wentworth is the naval officer who courts Anne Elliot in Jane Austen's Persuasion

explanation.surface: A good-for-nothing ship's captain has died.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Worthless' as worth-less: take WORTH from Austen's Captain WENTWORTH. The question mark admits the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To have left is to have gone away, the past tense of go.

clue.text: Article penned by Bacon — he translated apocalyptic story

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by, so the article goes inside the other letters
translated means turned into another form, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

parts.note: the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Francis Bacon writes an essay and translates a tale of the end of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bacon' suggests Francis Bacon the essayist, but it is plain anagram fodder with 'he', signalled by 'translated'; 'penned by' sets the article inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevil Shute's 1957 novel follows survivors in Australia awaiting the fallout of nuclear war.

clue.text: Kant adjusted position about knitwear

indicators.note: adjusted means altered, so the philosopher's name is rearranged
about means turned round, so the word for position is read backwards

parts.note: a spot is a place or position

explanation.surface: The philosopher Kant changes his stance on woollens.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeveless knitted pullovers are a type of knitted garment.

clue.text: Problem delved into by editor here?

definitions.text: Problem delved into by editor here?

indicators.note: delved into means entered, so the editor's abbreviation goes inside the word for a problem

parts.note: a rub is a difficulty, as in Hamlet's 'there's the rub'

explanation.surface: An editor digs into a fault, and this is the fix.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: a sound problem dug into by a film editor is fixed by dubbing the track again, and 'here?' points at that.
explanation.definitionFit: Re-recording a soundtrack is a film editor's usual cure for faulty dialogue.

clue.text: Georgian musicians make time for Dutch artist

parts.note: the rock band R.E.M. came from Athens, Georgia
a make of goods is a brand

explanation.surface: A band from the American South supposedly set aside time to study a Dutch master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Georgian' suggests the Caucasus or Britain's Georgian era, but it means the US state of Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Golden Age painter of The Night Watch, the most famous artist of the Netherlands.

clue.text: Like meeting point in US city Corleone, say, rejected

indicators.note: rejected things are sent back, so the run of pieces is read from the end to the start

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
Vito Corleone of The Godfather is a Mafia don, an example of the title

explanation.surface: A Mafia boss gets turned away at a rendezvous in an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a point where lines or paths meet, and the adjective for a node describes such a junction.

clue.text: Flog cover of book displaying tropical fish

parts.note: to leather someone is to beat them with a strap
a dust jacket is the paper cover of a hardback book

explanation.surface: Selling a book on the strength of its cover reveals an exotic fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flog' looks like 'sell', but it means to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Filefish of warm seas are known by this name for their tough skin.

clue.text: Reports avoiding a new name for Cats

indicators.note: avoiding means leaving out, so the named letters are taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to report news is to announce it, and 'reports' as a verb is announces

explanation.surface: A sly nod to Eliot's poem about giving cats proper names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'name for Cats' recalls T. S. Eliot's 'The Naming of Cats' (source of the musical Cats), but 'Cats' alone is the definition, the big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a big cat of Central Asia.

clue.text: Brave novel about Irish broadcaster showing a bit of backbone

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round the other
novel means new and different, so the letters of brave are made into a new order

parts.note: RTE is Raidió Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's national broadcaster

explanation.surface: A review praising Huxley's Brave New World for its courage on Irish television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave novel' looks like Huxley's Brave New World, but 'novel' is the anagram signal, giving VEBRA, and 'about' wraps that round the broadcaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The spine is built from many small bones, each one a single unit of the backbone.

clue.text: What made the second Mrs de Winter abruptly mention one in anger

definitions.text: What made the second Mrs de Winter

indicators.note: abruptly means cut off short, so the word for mention loses its last letter

parts.note: to mention is to remark

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the word for anger

parts.note: rage is fury or anger
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Asks what made du Maurier's narrator a wife, voiced as a sudden furious outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: In du Maurier's Rebecca the unnamed narrator becomes the second Mrs de Winter by marrying the widower Maxim.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxim de Winter's second wedding is what turned the narrator into the second Mrs de Winter.

clue.text: Dangerous driver dragged to hearing

indicators.note: to hearing means as it sounds to a listener, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a car being dragged behind a truck is towed

explanation.surface: A reckless motorist is hauled off to a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Toad of Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows is a notoriously reckless motorist; 'hearing' looks like a court case but signals the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Grahame's Toad of Toad Hall crashes car after car, the classic literary road hog.

clue.text: Gunners record being loud, then always quiet before long

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
ever means always, as in for ever
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A football club's chronicle of noisy matches followed by endless hush.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gunners are Arsenal, the London football club; 'record' looks like a statistic but is a written account.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Hornby's memoir chronicles his life as an Arsenal supporter, so it is literally a record of the Gunners.

clue.text: Everdene, extremely hot, sure to change Oak's meeting place?

indicators.note: to change means to alter, so these letters are rearranged
extremely picks the extreme letters, the first and last of the heroine's surname

explanation.surface: Bathsheba Everdene, feeling the heat, moves her rendezvous with Gabriel Oak in Far from the Madding Crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Gabriel Oak and Bathsheba Everdene are Hardy's lovers, but read 'Oak' as a tree: the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A hut built in the branches is a place where an oak could, jokingly, hold its meetings.

clue.text: Content of Holmes' cap is my reason for reading

indicators.note: the content of something is what lies inside it, so the answer is found inside these words

explanation.surface: A reader admits that the deerstalker of Sherlock Holmes is why they open the book.
explanation.definitionFit: Many readers turn to fiction to slip away from everyday life into another world.

clue.text: Racist seen circulating alternative history

indicators.note: circulating means moving round, so the letters of the two words go round into a new order

explanation.surface: A bigot is spotted doing the rounds of the neighbourhood.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen Sheers's novel imagines Britain under German occupation after a successful invasion, a counterfactual account of the war.

clue.text: King who wrote nonsense

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's tragic monarch who divides his kingdom among his daughters
Edward ..., the Victorian author of nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat

explanation.surface: A monarch who produced drivel.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to Shakespeare's tragic king and to Edward Lear, master of nonsense verse.

clue.text: Rhyming perhaps recalled reference work

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the two pieces are read backwards

parts.note: to cite is to refer to a source
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A reference book about rhyme is withdrawn by its publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reference work' looks like a dictionary, but it is two pieces, CITE and OP.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme is one feature of verse, so rhyming is an example of being verse-like.

clue.text: Keen to cover Hello, Goodbye, abandoning end theme of Don Quixote

indicators.note: to cover means to go over and around, so one piece wraps the rest

parts.note: to keen is to wail in grief, to cry
hi is a greeting

indicators.note: abandoning end means the final letter is dropped from the word for goodbye

parts.note: vale is Latin for farewell

explanation.surface: Song titles from the Beatles get set against the core subject of Cervantes's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hello, Goodbye' looks like the Beatles song, but it is two words: HI and VALE, cut to VAL by 'abandoning end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cervantes's novel satirises the ideals of knightly romance that the old man tries to live by.

clue.text: Odd pages removed from Passage to India over specks

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the whole run is read backwards
removed from means taken out, so those letters leave the word passage

parts.note: the letters of pages, oddly arranged, are the letters to take out
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Stray pages have been torn from a copy of Forster's A Passage to India, leaving tiny flecks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage to India' looks like Forster's title, but it is three pieces. 'Odd' rearranges 'pages' so its letters can be struck from the first word, leaving SA; 'over' reverses SATOI.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest Greek letter gives a word for a tiny amount, so these are small specks.

clue.text: Ridicule Fanthorpe's opening book

parts.note: to josh someone is to tease or make fun of them
the poet wrote as U. A. Fanthorpe, so her name opens with the initials U and A

explanation.surface: Mocking the first poem in a collection by the poet Fanthorpe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' tempts you to take only F, but the poet published as U. A. Fanthorpe, and her name begins with those initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixth book of the Old Testament tells of Moses's successor and the fall of Jericho.

clue.text: Wilder heroine netting bachelor

parts.note: a web is a net, a mesh of threads
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in degrees

explanation.surface: Thornton Wilder's leading lady catches herself an unmarried man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'netting' looks like a container signal, but it is the noun, WEB. Emily Webb is the heroine of Thornton Wilder's play Our Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily is the girl at the centre of Thornton Wilder's Our Town, so she is his heroine.

clue.text: Tense adaptation of Titus, incompletely playing for everyone

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: an adaptation reworks its source, so the letters are rearranged
incompletely means the name is cut short, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A stage adaptation of Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus is played under strain, never quite finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titus' suggests Shakespeare's Roman tragedy; 'incompletely' docks its last letter and 'adaptation of' rearranges what is left to UTTI.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the Italian direction marks a passage where the whole ensemble plays together.

clue.text: Amazed gathering around ball behind a resident of Rosmersholm

indicators.note: behind places the rugby piece after the rest in the answer

parts.note: Rebecca West lives at Rosmersholm, the house in Ibsen's play of that name
in rugby a ruck forms when players gather round the ball on the ground

explanation.surface: An awed crowd gathers round the ball near a character from an Ibsen drama.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruck is a rugby term for players gathered over the ball on the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Being overwhelmed with wonder is the same as being amazed.

clue.text: Keats club meet extraordinary Irish poet

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of the ordinary, so the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A Keats society holds a meeting with a remarkable poet from Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dublin-born writer is best known for plays and novels but also published poetry.
